# Concepts

*xxxx* –\> would be the name of the file/ thing that we want to look for, this is an example

## Formats for storing sequence information

### Fasta

It is a sequence format that is often used for reference data. It doesn't have quality scores so assumed to be correct

It is used for nucleotide and protein data

The fasta format consists of 1 or more entries each of which consists of a header and a sequence

Used for a wide variety of sequence types including whole genomes, transcriptomes, proteins. Each entry has a title line and a sequence. Multiple entries can be stored in a single file

- Title. One line. Begins with \>

- Sequence Identifier (name after the title)

- Sequence. Under the title in another line. Can be many lines

### Fastq

Most commonly used for "raw" reads from next generation sequencing experiments. Includes quality scores for every base.

The `fastq` format is designed for storing sequencing data along with quality scores.

Like FASTA but with additional information about the reliability of each base.

Mostly used to store outputs from sequencing instruments. Each entry has exactly four lines. Often millions of entries in a single file.

- Line 1: Identifier Begins with \@

- Sequence identifier . Name that goes after \@

- Line 2: Sequence

- Line 3: Description Begins with +

- Line 4: Quality Scores

It is a standard format used for many types of sequencing including Illumina short reads and longer reads produced by Nanopore or PacBio sequencing.

Each read occupies 4 lines in a fastq file. The lines are as follows;

1.  Starts with `@` and contains a unique identifier for the sequence

2.  Is the sequence itself

3.  Starts with `+` and almost always nothing else

4.  Contains quality scores. These are encoded using ASCII characters with one character per base.

The full list of quality score letters from 0-93 is

```         
!"#$%&'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ[\]^_`abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{|}~
```

# Working directory:

## mkdir

it works for creating a new working directory

## pwd (print working directory)

If we send the terminal this it will show us our working directory

## cd (change directory)

- *cd xxxx/* –\> will open a new folder/ document in the directory that we are, meaning that we will change the directory to that one

  example: we will go from /home/jd163481/mb5370-workshops to /home/jd163481/mb5370-workshops/command_line if we put *cd command_line/*

- *cd ..* we will go back one step in the directory

  example: we will go from /home/jd163481/mb5370-workshops/command_line to /home/jd163481/mb5370-workshops if we put *cd ..*

# Files:

## cat

command used to see files, you put *cat xxxx*

## head

to only see the first lines of the file we use the command head

Example: we only want to see the first 2 lines

*head -2 xxxx*

## grep (**g**lobally search a **r**egular **e**xpression and **p**rint)

finds lines matching specific strings in files

- if we want to find the header –\> *grep '\^\>' xxxx*

- specific text in the document (for example aminoacid sequences) –\> *grep KDRNKK xxxx*

  it will show in red the sequence

- if we put *-n* before the sequence it will show the line number where the match is –\> *grep -n KDRNKK xxxx*

  result: *3:LTTLEVAEADVDSTLETM**KDRNKK**NSAKLSKIGNNMKSL*

- ***man** grep* –\> to see all the flags (commands) of grep. his favourites:

  - -i -\> case insensitive match

  - -n -\> report line number of matches

  - -c -\> count all files that contain the pattern

  - -w -\> match whole words only
